facts.fact: A Snowflake organization is a first-class object linking all accounts owned by one business entity, used for account management, billing, replication/failover and data sharing (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/organizations).

Snowflake, not the customer, creates the organization when the first account is provisioned, after which more accounts can be created self-service (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/organizations).

A Snowflake organization can contain a Snowflake organization account, regular accounts (including trials) and Snowflake Open Catalog accounts; the organization account serves organization administrators and premium views in the `ORGANIZATION_USAGE` schema (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/organizations).
The Snowflake organization account became GA on 2025-01-27 (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/2025/other/2025-01-27-org-account).
Snowflake Open Catalog accounts can be part of a Snowflake organization (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/organizations).
Each Snowflake account lives on one cloud (AWS, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud) in one region, chosen independently per account (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-cloud-platforms).
Snowflake accounts can run on AWS (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-cloud-platforms).
Snowflake accounts can run on Microsoft Azure (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-cloud-platforms).
Snowflake accounts can run on Google Cloud (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-cloud-platforms).
Snowflake credit and storage prices vary by region and cloud platform, and mixing platforms can add data-transfer charges (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-cloud-platforms).
Snowflake editions are Standard, Enterprise, Business Critical and Virtual Private Snowflake (VPS), each a superset of the previous one (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).
Snowflake Enterprise edition adds multi-cluster warehouses, Time Travel up to 90 days, and masking and row access policies (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).
Snowflake Business Critical edition adds PrivateLink, Tri-Secret Secure, HIPAA/PCI DSS support, failover/failback and client redirect (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).
Virtual Private Snowflake (VPS) runs in a fully separate environment with no Marketplace listings (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).

The Snowflake editions page lists Cortex AI Functions, Cortex Analyst, Cortex Fine-tuning and Cortex Search for all four editions with no edition gating, so Standard edition suffices (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).
Cortex Analyst is listed for all four Snowflake editions, including Standard (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).
Cortex Fine-tuning is listed for all four Snowflake editions, including Standard (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).
Cortex Search is listed for all four Snowflake editions, including Standard (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).
Cortex AI Guardrails needs Snowflake Enterprise edition or higher (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).

The preferred Snowflake account identifier is `orgname-account_name` with URL `https://<orgname>-<account_name>.snowflakecomputing.com`; the legacy account locator form is `<locator>.<cloud_region_id>.<cloud>.snowflakecomputing.com` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-account-identifier).

Snowflake account names may contain underscores, and Snowflake also accepts the hyphenated variant, which is required for Okta SSO and SCIM (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-account-identifier).

Snowflake self-service trials last 30 days or until the free balance runs out, then the account is suspended; upgrading moves the account to On Demand billing (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-trial-account).
AI features are disabled by default on Snowflake self-service trials and are enabled by adding a credit card (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-trial-account).

Day-one asks for an engineer on a Snowflake engagement (synthesis): the account identifier (`orgname-account_name`) and URL (public or PrivateLink); a PERSON user with SSO and MFA; a custom role with the needed `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_*` database roles and `USAGE` on the target database, schema and warehouse; a SERVICE or SERVICE_AGENT user for the agent runtime with its auth method (key pair, WIF or PAT plus a network policy); the value of `CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION`; and whether `CORTEX_USER` and `USE AI FUNCTIONS` were revoked from PUBLIC (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).

Snowflake user `TYPE` values are `PERSON`, `SERVICE`, `LEGACY_SERVICE`, `SERVICE_AGENT`, `SNOWFLAKE_SERVICE` and `NULL` (treated as PERSON) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-user-management).
Snowflake PERSON users are humans who must enroll in MFA (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-user-management).
SNOWFLAKE_SERVICE users are created by Snowflake for Snowpark Container Services and cannot be created or assigned by admins (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-user-management).

Snowflake `TYPE = SERVICE` users cannot use passwords or MFA, cannot have `FIRST_NAME`, `LAST_NAME`, `PASSWORD`, `MUST_CHANGE_PASSWORD` or `MINS_TO_BYPASS_MFA`, and are not subject to authentication-policy MFA enforcement (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-user-management).
Snowflake SERVICE users authenticate with key pair, OAuth, workload identity federation or programmatic access tokens (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-user-management).
Snowflake SERVICE users can authenticate with OAuth (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-user-management).
Snowflake SERVICE users can authenticate with workload identity federation (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-user-management).
Snowflake SERVICE users can authenticate with programmatic access tokens (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-user-management).

Snowflake `TYPE = SERVICE_AGENT` is a user type for an autonomous AI agent acting under its own identity; it can be managed via SQL or SCIM (`type = service_agent`), and every session it opens is agent-active (`SYS_CONTEXT('SNOWFLAKE$CURRENT','IS_AGENT_ACTIVATED')` returns `'TRUE'`) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).
Snowflake SERVICE_AGENT users cannot use passwords or SAML SSO, and the release status of the user type is not stated on the page (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-user-management).
Snowflake SERVICE_AGENT users support workload identity federation (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).
Snowflake SERVICE_AGENT users support key pair authentication (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).
Snowflake SERVICE_AGENT users support programmatic access tokens (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).

facts.fact: Snowflake agent identity distinguishes delegated agents (acting for a user) from autonomous agents (own SERVICE_AGENT identity) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).
Cortex Agents, Cortex lite agents, CoCo clients, Snowflake CoWork and Snowflake-managed MCP servers are marked agentic automatically (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).
Snowflake CoWork sessions are marked agentic automatically by Snowflake agent identity (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).
Snowflake-managed MCP server sessions are marked agentic automatically (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).
Custom Snowflake OAuth or External OAuth integrations are marked agentic with `IS_AGENTIC = TRUE` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).
A Snowflake PAT alone does not make a delegated session agentic (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).
Snowflake OAuth token exchange issues per-task delegated tokens for agents per RFC 8693 (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-token-exchange).

Snowflake token exchange is a POST to `https://<account_identifier>.snowflakecomputing.com/oauth/token` with `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange`, a `subject_token` (OAuth access token, PAT or WIF), optional `scope=session:role:<role>`, `authorization_details` with a Restricted Session Scope (`snowflake-rss.v1`) and `act={"sub":"...","type":"agent"}` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-token-exchange).
Snowflake exchanged tokens last one hour by default, have no refresh token and cannot be re-exchanged; release status is not stated (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-token-exchange).

Snowflake does not authenticate the caller of token exchange and does not verify `act`: anyone holding a valid subject token can exchange it, so the subject token must stay in the trusted app tier, and the self-asserted `act` must not be used for access control (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-token-exchange).

Single-factor password sign-in is retired in three phases: Phase 1 (Sep 2025 to Jan 2026, bundle 2025_06) requires MFA for password sign-in to Snowsight; Phase 2 (May to Jul 2026, rolling) requires a second factor for new human users on all surfaces and `SERVICE` for new non-human users; Phase 3 (Aug to Oct 2026, rolling) ends human password-only sign-in and blocks non-human users from passwords; dates vary per account and may be extended (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-mfa-rollout).

Snowflake `LEGACY_SERVICE` is deprecated: after Phase 2 it cannot be assigned in `CREATE USER` or `ALTER USER`, and in Phase 3 (Aug to Oct 2026) existing LEGACY_SERVICE users are migrated to `SERVICE` and blocked from passwords (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-mfa-rollout).
Existing Snowflake LEGACY_SERVICE users are migrated to `SERVICE` in Phase 3 (Aug to Oct 2026) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-user-management).
Snowflake MFA methods are passkeys (recommended), TOTP authenticator apps and Duo (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-mfa).

Enforce Snowflake MFA with an authentication policy using `MFA_ENROLLMENT = 'REQUIRED'`, restrict methods with `MFA_POLICY (ALLOWED_METHODS = ...)`, and require MFA after SSO with `MFA_POLICY (ENFORCE_MFA_ON_EXTERNAL_AUTHENTICATION = 'ALL')` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-mfa).
Snowflake `ALLOW_CLIENT_MFA_CACHING` caches MFA tokens up to four hours (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-mfa).

Snowflake authentication policies control `AUTHENTICATION_METHODS`, `CLIENT_TYPES`, `SECURITY_INTEGRATIONS`, MFA, `PAT_POLICY` and `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_POLICY`; a user-level policy overrides the account-level one, and by default all methods and clients are allowed (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/authentication-policies).
Creating a Snowflake authentication policy needs `CREATE AUTHENTICATION POLICY` on a schema (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/authentication-policies).
Applying a Snowflake authentication policy needs SECURITYADMIN or `APPLY AUTHENTICATION POLICY` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/authentication-policies).
Snowflake authentication policy `CLIENT_TYPES` is best-effort and does not restrict REST API access (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/workload-identity-federation).

Snowflake human SSO supports SAML 2.0 (`TYPE = SAML2`); Okta and Microsoft Entra ID have native SAML support and other SAML IdPs need a custom app (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-security-fed-auth-overview).

Snowflake supports OIDC sign-in with managed providers Google and Entra ID and custom OIDC including Okta, PingFederate, Auth0 and Keycloak (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-security-fed-auth-overview).
Snowflake drivers use `authenticator=OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_CODE` for OIDC SSO, not `externalbrowser` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-security-fed-auth-overview).

Snowflake SCIM provisioning supports Okta (`OKTA_PROVISIONER`), Microsoft Entra ID (`AAD_PROVISIONER`) and custom IdPs (`GENERIC_SCIM_PROVISIONER`) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/scim-intro).
Create Okta SCIM with `CREATE SECURITY INTEGRATION ... TYPE = SCIM SCIM_CLIENT = 'okta' RUN_AS_ROLE = 'OKTA_PROVISIONER'` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/scim-okta).
Snowflake SCIM provisioning supports Microsoft Entra ID via the `AAD_PROVISIONER` role (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/scim-intro).
Okta SCIM provisioning runs as `OKTA_PROVISIONER` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/scim-okta).
Microsoft Entra ID SCIM provisioning runs as `AAD_PROVISIONER` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/scim-intro).
Custom-IdP SCIM provisioning runs as `GENERIC_SCIM_PROVISIONER` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/scim-intro).
The Snowflake SCIM provisioner role must own the users and roles it manages and needs `CREATE USER` and `CREATE ROLE` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/scim-intro).

Snowflake key pair authentication needs at least a 2048-bit RSA key, and two public keys (`RSA_PUBLIC_KEY`, `RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_2`) allow rotation (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/key-pair-auth).

Named key pairs (`ALTER USER ... ADD KEY PAIR`) are now recommended because `RSA_PUBLIC_KEY` supports neither role restriction nor expiration; verify with `DESC USER` `RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_FP` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/key-pair-auth).

Snowflake workload identity federation gives SERVICE and SERVICE_AGENT users keyless auth from AWS IAM roles, Microsoft Entra ID / Azure managed identities, Google Cloud service accounts and OIDC issuers, with OIDC covering EKS, AKS, GKE, GitHub Actions and GitLab (customised `sub` claim) and SPIFFE/SPIRE (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/workload-identity-federation).

Configure Snowflake WIF with `CREATE USER ... WORKLOAD_IDENTITY = (TYPE = AWS|AZURE|GCP|OIDC ...)`; drivers use `authenticator='WORKLOAD_IDENTITY'` plus `workload_identity_provider` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/workload-identity-federation).

facts.fact: Configuring WIF on another Snowflake user needs `OWNERSHIP` or `MODIFY PROGRAMMATIC AUTHENTICATION METHODS` on that user (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/workload-identity-federation).
Configuring PATs on another Snowflake user needs `OWNERSHIP` or `MODIFY PROGRAMMATIC AUTHENTICATION METHODS` on that user (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/programmatic-access-tokens).

Snowflake PATs work for PERSON, SERVICE and SERVICE_AGENT users, authenticate the REST APIs, SQL API, SCIM API, Snowpark Container Services and Horizon Catalog endpoint, and replace the password in drivers (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/programmatic-access-tokens).

REST calls with a Snowflake PAT send `Authorization: Bearer <token>` with optional `X-Snowflake-Authorization-Token-Type: PROGRAMMATIC_ACCESS_TOKEN` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/programmatic-access-tokens).
The Snowflake SQL API accepts programmatic access tokens (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/programmatic-access-tokens).

Snowflake PAT lifetime defaults to 15 days with a 365-day maximum, and each user can hold up to 15 tokens; set per token with `DAYS_TO_EXPIRY` or per policy with `PAT_POLICY` `DEFAULT_EXPIRY_IN_DAYS` / `MAX_EXPIRY_IN_DAYS` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/programmatic-access-tokens).
Manage Snowflake PATs with `ALTER USER ... ADD | ROTATE | REMOVE PROGRAMMATIC ACCESS TOKEN` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/programmatic-access-tokens).

Snowflake SERVICE users must be subject to a network policy to generate or use a PAT, SERVICE_AGENT users need none, and PERSON users can generate a PAT without one but need one to authenticate (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/programmatic-access-tokens).

`ROLE_RESTRICTION` is required by default for SERVICE and SERVICE_AGENT PATs, and `BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST` can stop roles such as ACCOUNTADMIN being used (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/programmatic-access-tokens).

Snowflake OAuth (`TYPE = OAUTH`) uses the authorization code flow with browser consent and supports partner clients (Tableau, Looker, Alation, ThoughtSpot) and `OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-snowflake-overview).
Snowflake OAuth's documented grant types are only `authorization_code` and `refresh_token`, and access tokens last about 10 minutes (https://docs.snowflake.com/user-guide/oauth-custom).
Snowflake External OAuth (`TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH`) suits programmatic clients, while Snowflake OAuth uses browser consent (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-intro).
Snowflake External OAuth supports Okta as an authorization server (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-ext-overview).
Snowflake External OAuth supports Microsoft Entra ID as an authorization server (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-ext-overview).
Snowflake External OAuth supports PingFederate and custom authorization servers (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-ext-overview).

Snowflake External OAuth maps roles from scopes `session:role:<role>` or `session:role-any` (needs `EXTERNAL_OAUTH_ANY_ROLE_MODE`), maps users via `EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TOKEN_USER_MAPPING_CLAIM` and `EXTERNAL_OAUTH_SNOWFLAKE_USER_MAPPING_ATTRIBUTE`, and is the documented path for client-credentials machine-to-machine flows (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-ext-overview).

Snowflake OAuth blocks ACCOUNTADMIN, ORGADMIN, GLOBALORGADMIN and SECURITYADMIN by default; unblock with `OAUTH_ADD_PRIVILEGED_ROLES_TO_BLOCKED_LIST = FALSE` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-snowflake-overview).

Snowflake External OAuth blocks ACCOUNTADMIN, ORGADMIN, GLOBALORGADMIN and SECURITYADMIN by default; unblock with `EXTERNAL_OAUTH_ADD_PRIVILEGED_ROLES_TO_BLOCKED_LIST = FALSE` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/oauth-ext-overview).

Snowflake added a built-in `SNOWFLAKE$LOCAL_APPLICATION` OAuth integration for local applications (release note 2026-01-21) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/2026/other/2026-01-21-snowflake-oauth-local-applications).
Snowflake REST APIs, including Cortex Agents, accept PATs (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).
Snowflake REST APIs, including Cortex Agents, accept key-pair JWTs (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).
Snowflake REST APIs, including Cortex Agents, accept OAuth (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).

Cortex Agents are called through Snowflake REST APIs, where `X-Snowflake-Role` sets the role and otherwise the user's default role applies (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).
The Snowflake-managed MCP server defaults to Snowflake OAuth, and OAuth sessions use the user's `DEFAULT_ROLE` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-mcp).
The Snowflake-managed MCP server supports External OAuth (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-mcp).

The Snowflake-managed MCP server accepts PATs, but Snowflake recommends OAuth over hard-coded tokens and a least-privileged role for any PAT (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-mcp).

Snowflake combines discretionary access control (owners), role-based access control and user-based access control; a session has one primary role (which alone authorizes `CREATE`) plus any number of secondary roles (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).
In Snowflake UBAC, privileges granted directly to users count only when `USE SECONDARY ROLES` is `ALL` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).

Snowflake system roles are GLOBALORGADMIN, ORGADMIN, ACCOUNTADMIN, SECURITYADMIN, USERADMIN, SYSADMIN and PUBLIC; ACCOUNTADMIN contains SYSADMIN and SECURITYADMIN (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).
Snowflake SECURITYADMIN holds `MANAGE GRANTS` and inherits USERADMIN (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).
Snowflake USERADMIN holds `CREATE USER` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).
Snowflake USERADMIN holds `CREATE ROLE` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).
Snowflake SYSADMIN creates warehouses and databases (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).
The Snowflake PUBLIC role is granted to every user and role (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).

Snowflake GLOBALORGADMIN in the organization account replaces ORGADMIN, which is being phased out for multi-account organizations (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/organization-administrators).
Snowflake ORGADMIN can be enabled in up to eight accounts by default (`ALTER ACCOUNT <name> SET IS_ORG_ADMIN = TRUE`) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/organization-administrators).

Snowflake promises at least three months' email notice before removing ORGADMIN, and no removal date was published as of 2026-11-14 (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/organization-administrators).

facts.fact: Snowflake recommends custom roles rolled up to SYSADMIN; without the roll-up, SYSADMIN cannot manage objects owned by the custom role (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).
Snowflake recommends that custom roles be created by USERADMIN (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).

Snowflake database roles are scoped to one database and cannot be activated directly or granted directly to users; grant them to an account role (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).

Snowflake Native App providers define application roles, and `SNOWFLAKE.PUBLIC` and `SNOWFLAKE.APP_PUBLIC` are managed automatically (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).

Calling Snowflake Cortex AI Functions needs the account privilege `USE AI FUNCTIONS` (or per-function `USE AI FUNCTION <name>`) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).
Calling Cortex AI Functions also needs database role `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` or `SNOWFLAKE.AI_FUNCTIONS_USER` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).
`SNOWFLAKE.AI_FUNCTIONS_USER` is an alternative to `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` for calling Cortex AI Functions (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).

`USE AI FUNCTIONS` is granted to PUBLIC by default and managed by ACCOUNTADMIN, for example `REVOKE USE AI FUNCTIONS ON ACCOUNT FROM ROLE PUBLIC;` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).

The `USE AI FUNCTIONS` privilege was introduced in a 2026-02-20 release note, and per-function privileges reached GA on 2026-05-13 (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/2026/other/2026-02-20-use-ai-functions-privilege).

`SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` covers all Covered AI Features, including Cortex Agents, AI Functions, Cortex Search and CoWork (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).
`SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` grants access to Cortex AI Functions (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).
`SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` grants access to Cortex Search (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).
`SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` grants access to Snowflake CoWork (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).

`SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` is granted to PUBLIC by default; revoke with `REVOKE DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER FROM ROLE PUBLIC;`, though revoking does not block ACCOUNTADMIN (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/opting-out).
`SNOWFLAKE.AI_FUNCTIONS_USER` is GA since 2026-04-02 (https://docs.snowflake.com/release-notes/2026/other/2026-04-02-ai-functions-user-db-role).

`SNOWFLAKE.AI_FUNCTIONS_USER` covers scalar AI functions only, excluding `AI_AGG` and `AI_SUMMARIZE_AGG`, and is not granted to PUBLIC (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).

`SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_EMBED_USER` covers `AI_EMBED`, `EMBED_TEXT_768`, `EMBED_TEXT_1024` and Cortex Search services with managed embeddings, and is not granted to PUBLIC (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).

Snowflake model-level RBAC uses application roles in the SNOWFLAKE application, such as `SNOWFLAKE."CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-ALL"` and per-model `CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-<model>`; model objects live in `SNOWFLAKE.MODELS` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).

Snowflake model objects are refreshed daily by `SNOWFLAKE.MODELS.CORTEX_BASE_MODELS_REFRESH_TASK`, or on demand with `CALL SNOWFLAKE.MODELS.CORTEX_BASE_MODELS_REFRESH();` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).

Accounts with allowlist `'All'` get `CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-ALL` via `SNOWFLAKE.PUBLIC`, removable only with `CALL SNOWFLAKE.LOCAL.REVOKE_FROM_PUBLIC_APPLICATION_ROLE('APP_ROLE','CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-ALL');` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/bcr-bundles/un-bundled/bcr-2378).
ACCOUNTADMIN always has Cortex model access regardless of model RBAC (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).

Snowflake `CORTEX_MODELS_ALLOWLIST` is being retired in favour of model RBAC: from 2026-08-05 it can only be set to `'None'`, a one-time migration ran 2026-08-17 to 2026-09-04, and full retirement is January 2027; dates are subject to change (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/bcr-bundles/un-bundled/bcr-2378).

Allowlist-based Cortex model control was removed on 2026-09-08 via bundle 2026_07, which RBAC-enforces embedding models (AI_EMBED, Cortex Search) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/bcr-bundles/un-bundled/bcr-2378).
Calling Snowflake Cortex Agents needs `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` or `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_AGENT_USER` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).
`SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_AGENT_USER` is sufficient to call Cortex Agents but excludes Cortex Analyst (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).
`SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_AGENT_USER` excludes Cortex Analyst, so add `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_ANALYST_USER` for agent Analyst tools (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).

Cortex Analyst tools in Cortex Agents need `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_ANALYST_USER` when the caller has only `CORTEX_AGENT_USER` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).

Snowflake Cortex Agent object privileges are `CREATE AGENT` (schema), `USAGE`, `MODIFY`, `MONITOR` and `OWNERSHIP` (agent); temporary agents do not need `CREATE AGENT` (https://docs.snowflake.com/sql-reference/sql/create-agent).

Cortex Agent USAGE also needs USAGE on the database and schema, MONITOR shows threads, logs and traces, and `CREATE OR REPLACE` needs OWNERSHIP (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).

Cortex Agent tools need the caller's own grants: USAGE on Cortex Search services, USAGE on the database, schema and tables behind semantic views, USAGE on custom-tool functions and procedures, and USAGE on warehouses in the agent spec (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).

By default (`orchestration.tool_not_accessible = accept`) Cortex Agents skip inaccessible tools with warnings, while `reject` fails the run (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).

facts.fact: Snowflake Cortex Analyst needs `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` or `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_ANALYST_USER` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-analyst).
`SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_ANALYST_USER` is an alternative to `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` for Cortex Analyst (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-analyst).

Cortex Analyst also needs SELECT on referenced tables, USAGE on referenced Cortex Search services, and READ/WRITE on the stage holding a YAML semantic model (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-analyst).
ACCOUNTADMIN can disable Cortex Analyst account-wide with `ALTER ACCOUNT SET ENABLE_CORTEX_ANALYST = FALSE` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-analyst).

Creating a Snowflake Cortex Search service needs `CREATE CORTEX SEARCH SERVICE` on the schema, SELECT on sources, USAGE on the refresh warehouse, and CORTEX_USER or CORTEX_EMBED_USER; querying needs USAGE on the service, database and schema (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-search/cortex-search-overview).

Cortex Search services search with owner's rights; `OPERATE` suspends/resumes and `MONITOR` shows refresh history (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-search/cortex-search-overview).

Snowflake Intelligence was renamed Snowflake CoWork at Snowflake Summit, June 2026 (secondary for the rename date) (https://itbrief.com.au/story/snowflake-renames-ai-tools-amid-broader-platform-push).
Cortex Code was renamed Snowflake CoCo at Snowflake Summit, June 2026 (secondary for the rename date) (https://itbrief.com.au/story/snowflake-renames-ai-tools-amid-broader-platform-push).

Snowflake CoWork SQL keywords still use `SNOWFLAKE INTELLIGENCE`, and the `SNOWFLAKE_INTELLIGENCE.AGENTS` schema is deprecated for visibility in favour of the CoWork object (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/snowflake-cowork/deploy-agents).

The Snowflake CoWork object `SNOWFLAKE_INTELLIGENCE_OBJECT_DEFAULT` (one per account) controls which agents CoWork shows; agents are not added automatically (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/snowflake-cowork/deploy-agents).
`CREATE SNOWFLAKE INTELLIGENCE ON ACCOUNT` is held by ACCOUNTADMIN by default (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/snowflake-cowork/deploy-agents).

Grant `USAGE ON SNOWFLAKE INTELLIGENCE SNOWFLAKE_INTELLIGENCE_OBJECT_DEFAULT` and add agents with `ALTER SNOWFLAKE INTELLIGENCE ... ADD AGENT <db.schema.agent>` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/snowflake-cowork/deploy-agents).

Snowflake CoWork users need USAGE on the agent, its database and schema, plus tool grants (USAGE on search services and semantic views, READ on stages for citations, SELECT on tables), a default role and a default warehouse (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/snowflake-cowork/deploy-agents).

Restrict a Snowflake user to CoWork with `ALTER USER ... SET ALLOWED_INTERFACES = (SNOWFLAKE_INTELLIGENCE)` or the SCIM attribute `allowedInterfaces` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/snowflake-cowork/deploy-agents).

Snowflake CoWork Automations' `EXECUTE AGENT TASK` is granted to PUBLIC by default, while MANAGE ACCESS on Artifacts stops being granted to any role by default from late September 2026 (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/bcr-bundles/un-bundled/bcr-2349).
Snowflake-managed MCP server privileges are `CREATE MCP SERVER`, `OWNERSHIP`, `MODIFY` and `USAGE` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-mcp).

Snowflake-managed MCP server USAGE does not grant tool access; each tool needs its own grant, such as USAGE on a Cortex Search service, SELECT on a semantic view or USAGE on an agent (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-mcp).

The Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint is `https://<account_url>/api/v2/databases/{db}/schemas/{schema}/mcp-servers/{name}` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-mcp).

With Restricted Caller's Rights, `USE AI FUNCTIONS` must be granted to both the session role and the service or application owner role (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-privileges-and-access).

Least-privilege Snowflake agent runtime (synthesis): a SERVICE_AGENT (or SERVICE) user with WIF or key pair, a custom role holding `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_AGENT_USER` (plus `CORTEX_ANALYST_USER` if needed) and only the needed tool, warehouse, database and schema USAGE/SELECT grants, set as the PAT `ROLE_RESTRICTION` or OAuth scope (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-setup).

A least-privilege Cortex Agents runtime role holds `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_AGENT_USER` rather than `CORTEX_USER`, with ACCOUNTADMIN revoking `CORTEX_USER` and `USE AI FUNCTIONS` from PUBLIC (synthesis) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/programmatic-access-tokens).

In the least-privilege agent setup, USERADMIN creates the user and role, and SECURITYADMIN or the object owner grants privileges (synthesis) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).

SECURITYADMIN or the object owner grants the tool, warehouse, database and schema privileges for a Cortex Agents runtime role (synthesis) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/security-access-control-overview).
Snowflake masking, row access, projection, aggregation and join policies can check `IS_AGENT_ACTIVATED` to hide data from agent sessions (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).
`AGENT_RESTRICTED_SESSION_SCOPE` on a Snowflake session policy sets a privilege ceiling that applies only when an agent is active (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).

Snowflake network policies combine schema-level network rules into `ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULE_LIST` / `BLOCKED_NETWORK_RULE_LIST` for inbound access, with rule types including `IPV4`, `IPV6`, `AWSVPCEID`, `AZURELINKID` and `COMPUTE_POOL`; block wins, and security integration policies override user policies, which override account policies (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/network-policies).
Creating a Snowflake network policy needs SECURITYADMIN or `CREATE NETWORK POLICY` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/network-policies).
SECURITYADMIN can create Snowflake network policies (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/network-policies).

ACCOUNTADMIN authorizes Snowflake AWS PrivateLink with `SYSTEM$AUTHORIZE_PRIVATELINK` and gets endpoint details from `SYSTEM$GET_PRIVATELINK_CONFIG` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-security-privatelink).

Snowflake PrivateLink URLs take a `.privatelink.snowflakecomputing.com` form; Azure Private Link and Google Cloud Private Service Connect are documented separately (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-security-privatelink).
After testing Snowflake PrivateLink, block public access with a network policy (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-security-privatelink).

Snowflake `CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION` is set only by ACCOUNTADMIN with `ALTER ACCOUNT` and controls where Cortex inference may run (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cross-region-inference).

`CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION` values are `ANY_REGION`; `AWS_GLOBAL`, `AZURE_GLOBAL`, `GCP_GLOBAL`; `AWS_US`, `AWS_EU`, `AWS_APJ`, `AWS_JP`, `AWS_AU`, `AZURE_US`, `AZURE_EU`, `GCP_US` (combinable); or `DISABLED` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cross-region-inference).
ORGADMIN cannot set `CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cross-region-inference).

New Snowflake organizations created in commercial regions after 2026-03-09 default `CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION` to `ANY_REGION`, while other commercial accounts inherit a same-cloud geography value such as `AWS_US`; set it explicitly when residency matters (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cross-region-inference).
Check the setting with `SHOW PARAMETERS LIKE 'CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION' IN ACCOUNT;` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cross-region-inference).

Snowflake cross-region inference keeps stored data in the home region and does not persist prompts or responses in the processing region; same-cloud traffic stays on the provider backbone and cross-cloud traffic uses mTLS over the public internet; US Commercial Gov, FedRAMP High Plus and DoD regions stay in the US (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cross-region-inference).
Cross-region inference credits are charged in the requesting region with no egress fees (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cross-region-inference).

Snowflake says it never uses Customer Data to train models made available to its customer base, data is not available to other customers or model developers, and all AI models run inside Snowflake's security and governance perimeter except as the customer elects (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/guides-overview-ai-features).
Snowflake GA AI models get at least 60 days' notice before deprecation, and Preview models get none (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/guides-overview-ai-features).

facts.fact: The Snowflake AI Trust and Safety FAQ says inputs and outputs are not used to train models for other customers, stay in the Snowflake Security Boundary, and are not given to third-party model developers, except an explicit opt-in to Azure-hosted OpenAI GPT models for Cortex Analyst; fine-tuned models are usable only by the customer's account; the page returned HTTP 403 and claims are from search snippets (unverified) (https://www.snowflake.com/en/legal/compliance/snowflake-ai-trust-and-safety/).

Snowflake states that neither it nor frontier model providers (such as Anthropic) use Customer Data to train models, and that frontier models run on cloud-provider infrastructure (secondary; vendor blog) (https://www.snowflake.com/en/blog/engineering/cross-region-ai-inference-data-sovereignty/).

Snowflake Cortex Analyst does not train on Customer Data, sends only semantic model metadata to the LLM, and runs the generated SQL in the customer's warehouse (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-analyst).

Snowflake Cortex AI Functions are Covered AI Features when GA and Preview AI Features when in preview, under Snowflake's AI Terms and Acceptable Use Policy (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql).

Cortex AI Functions models come from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral AI, DeepSeek and xAI, deployed within the Snowflake Service perimeter (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql).
Snowflake Cortex Guard is GA since 2024-07-24 (https://docs.snowflake.com/release-notes/2024/other/2024-07-24-cortex-llm-updates).

Cortex Guard filters unsafe LLM output from `AI_COMPLETE` / `COMPLETE` when `guardrails: TRUE` is set in model options, and defaults to FALSE (https://docs.snowflake.com/sql-reference/functions/ai_complete-single-string).
Snowflake Cortex Guard is built on Meta Llama Guard 3 (https://docs.snowflake.com/sql-reference/functions/ai_complete-single-string).
Cortex Guard is billed on input tokens on top of the AI_COMPLETE charge (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-cost).

Snowflake Cortex AI Guardrails detect prompt injection (including indirect injection in tool outputs) and jailbreaks, with activity logged in `SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_AI_GUARDRAILS_USAGE_HISTORY` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-ai-guardrails).
Cortex AI Guardrails became GA for Cortex Code (now Snowflake CoCo) on 2026-04-20 (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/2026/other/2026-04-20-cortex-ai-guardrails-ga).
Cortex AI Guardrails became GA for Snowflake CoWork on 2026-05-14 (https://docs.snowflake.com/release-notes/2026/other/2026-05-14-cortex-ai-guardrails-si-cortex-agents).
Cortex AI Guardrails became GA for Cortex Agents on 2026-05-14 (https://docs.snowflake.com/release-notes/2026/other/2026-05-14-cortex-ai-guardrails-si-cortex-agents).

ACCOUNTADMIN enables Cortex AI Guardrails with `ALTER ACCOUNT SET AI_SETTINGS = $$ guardrails: advanced_prompt_injection: - enabled: true $$;` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-ai-guardrails).
Cortex AI Guardrails needs Enterprise edition or higher (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-ai-guardrails).

Cortex AI Guardrails needs cross-region inference set to `ANY_REGION`, `AWS_US`, `AWS_EU`, `AWS_JP`, `AWS_APJ` or `AWS_GLOBAL` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-ai-guardrails).

facts.fact: Snowflake Horizon Catalog's governed-AI pillar covers AI Guardrails that the page says detect, redact and block PII and PHI in agent outputs, and agents operate under the same RBAC policies as human users (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-horizon).
Snowflake Horizon groups data quality, classification, masking and row access policies, Access History and Trust Center (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-horizon).

Snowflake AI opt-out controls: revoke `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` and `SNOWFLAKE.COPILOT_USER` from PUBLIC; set `ENABLE_CORTEX_ANALYST = FALSE`; revoke `CREATE MODEL` (Fine-tuning) and `CREATE PROVISIONED THROUGHPUT`; or call `SELECT SYSTEM$DISABLE_FEATURE_GROUPS('AI_FEATURES');`, which is available on request through Snowflake Support (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/opting-out).
Revoking `SNOWFLAKE.COPILOT_USER` from PUBLIC is one of the Snowflake AI opt-out controls (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/opting-out).
Revoking `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER` from PUBLIC is one of the Snowflake AI opt-out controls (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/opting-out).

Snowflake audits agent activity in `QUERY_HISTORY.agent_type` (`CORTEX_AGENT`, `CORTEX_LITE_AGENT`, `EXTERNAL_AGENT`) and `ACCESS_HISTORY.agents_info` (the agent chain); OAuth logins appear in login history with `FIRST_AUTHENTICATION_FACTOR = OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/agent-identity).

Snowflake compliance attestations include SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001/27017/27018, PCI DSS, HIPAA (with a BAA), HITRUST CSF and FedRAMP Moderate and High, per an archived security addendum (secondary) (https://www.snowflake.com/en/legal/addenda/security-addendum/2024-10-01/).
Snowflake PCI, HITRUST and FedRAMP attestations apply to Business Critical and VPS, and FedRAMP only in certain US regions (secondary) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).
PCI, HITRUST and FedRAMP attestations apply to Virtual Private Snowflake (secondary) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/intro-editions).
The Snowflake-managed MCP server supports MCP revision 2025-11-25 (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-mcp).
The Snowflake-managed MCP server was not yet formally FedRAMP-assessed (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-mcp).

Snowflake bills AI features in AI Credits, which have one price regardless of edition or region and apply to the features in Table 6 of the Service Consumption Table: Cortex Code, Cortex Agents, Snowflake CoWork, Cortex REST API, Cortex AI Gateway, AI Functions, Cortex Search, Cortex Batch Search and AI Parse Doc (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/pricing).
Cortex Fine-tuning stays on legacy Platform Credits rather than AI Credits (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/pricing).
The Cortex Analyst API stays on legacy Platform Credits rather than AI Credits (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/pricing).

As shown on 2026-11-14, a Snowflake AI Credit costs $2.00 with global routing (`CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION` is `ANY_REGION`, `AWS_GLOBAL`, `GCP_GLOBAL` or `AZURE_GLOBAL`) and $2.20 with regional routing (`DISABLED` or a geography such as `AWS_US`) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/pricing).
Capacity discounts do not apply to Snowflake AI Credits, but automatic ACV-based AI Credit discounts do (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/pricing).

The Snowflake Service Consumption Table, the rate card for credits per million tokens, per message and per GB-month, is at https://www.snowflake.com/legal-files/CreditConsumptionTable.pdf (https://www.snowflake.com/legal-files/CreditConsumptionTable.pdf).
The Service Consumption Table PDF could not be parsed, so no per-model rates are quoted; a secondary source dates it 2026-09-30 (https://www.snowflake.com/legal-files/CreditConsumptionTable.pdf).

Snowflake Platform Credit price varies by edition and region, accounts buy On Demand or Capacity (pre-purchased) plans, and the docs' undated illustration uses $3.00 per Platform Credit for Enterprise (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/cost-understanding-overall).

Snowflake Gen1 standard warehouses burn 1 credit/hour at X-Small, doubling per size up to 512 at 6X-Large, billed per second with a 60-second minimum; Gen2 rates are in the Service Consumption Table (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/warehouses-overview).
Snowflake recommends warehouses no larger than MEDIUM for AI Functions because larger sizes do not help (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-cost).

Snowflake Cortex AI Functions are billed per million tokens (input and output), monitored in `CORTEX_AI_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY` and `METERING_DAILY_HISTORY` with `SERVICE_TYPE = 'AI_SERVICES'` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/governance-and-availability/ai-cost-management-and-governance).

The older Cortex cost page names the usage views `CORTEX_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY` and `CORTEX_FUNCTIONS_QUERY_USAGE_HISTORY`, while the newer governance page uses `CORTEX_AI_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-cost).

facts.fact: Snowflake Cortex Agents bill orchestration by tokens plus each tool's own cost: Analyst counts per token when called via Agents, Search bills index serving, custom tools bill warehouse time, and web search, code execution, MCP connectors and skills can add cost; usage is in `CORTEX_AGENT_USAGE_HISTORY` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents).

Snowflake Cortex Analyst bills per successful (HTTP 200) message, plus warehouse time for the generated SQL; usage is in `CORTEX_ANALYST_USAGE_HISTORY` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-analyst).

Snowflake Cortex Search bills serving per GB-month of uncompressed indexed data while the service is available, plus embedding tokens for changed rows, refresh warehouse time and storage (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-search/cortex-search-overview).

Snowflake CoWork usage is recorded in `SNOWFLAKE_COWORK_USAGE_HISTORY` (service type `SNOWFLAKE_INTELLIGENCE`) in tokens and tools (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/governance-and-availability/ai-cost-management-and-governance).

Snowflake per-user quotas cap AI spend per user and can block requests within minutes of hitting the limit; domains are `AI FUNCTION`, `SNOWFLAKE INTELLIGENCE`, `CORTEX AGENT`, `CORTEX CODE`, `AI GATEWAY` and `WAREHOUSE` (block applies only to AI domains) (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/budgets/per-user-quotas).
Creating a Snowflake per-user quota needs `SNOWFLAKE.QUOTA_CREATOR` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/budgets/per-user-quotas).
Creating a Snowflake per-user quota needs `CREATE SNOWFLAKE.CORE.QUOTA` (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/budgets/per-user-quotas).

Snowflake resource and shared resource budgets act within up to 8 hours (2 hours latency-optimized), unlike per-user quotas (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/governance-and-availability/ai-cost-management-and-governance).
GA status of Snowflake per-user quotas conflicts between sources (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/budgets/per-user-quotas).
